title: RDBMS Landscape & Dialects
html:
All major databases share core SQL, but each adds its own types, functions and syntax. Knowing the differences saves hours when you switch engines.

RDBMS — Relational Database Management System — the software that stores tables, enforces constraints, runs queries and manages transactions and users.

The major engines

EngineTypical useNotable traits
MySQL / MariaDBWeb apps (LAMP), SaaS back endsOpen source, InnoDB engine, very popular, replication-friendly
PostgreSQLGeneral purpose, analytics, GISMost standards-compliant open-source engine; rich types (JSONB, arrays), extensions
SQL ServerMicrosoft / enterprise stacksT-SQL dialect, strong tooling, TOP, IDENTITY
OracleLarge enterprises, bankingPL/SQL, ROWNUM, DUAL, powerful but commercial
SQLiteMobile apps, browsers, embedded, testsA library, not a server — the whole DB is one file; dynamic typing
About these notes

Every runnable example in these notes executes on SQLite 3.53, which supports modern SQL: CTEs, window functions, RIGHT/FULL joins, UPSERT, RETURNING and JSON. Where another engine differs, the variant is shown and labelled.

Do

Prefer standard features (COALESCE, CASE, FETCH FIRST, || or CONCAT) when they exist — the code ports more easily between engines.

Which SQL database should you choose for a new project?

Default to PostgreSQL for a general server-side app (standards, JSONB, extensions). MySQL is equally fine and widely hosted. SQLite for embedded/mobile/local tools and tests. SQL Server or Oracle usually when the organisation already runs them.

Is SQLite a “real” database?

Yes — it is fully transactional (ACID) and is the most deployed database in the world (every phone and browser). What it lacks is a server: no network access, no user accounts/GRANT, and one writer at a time. It is ideal for local data, not for many concurrent writers.
